description.short: Statalytics is a Discord integration for viewing neatly rendered game statistics for the popular Minecraft minigame, Bedwars.

long.heading: Tooling
long.content:
Statalytics is a Discord integration that provides an interface for viewing game stats for the popular Minecraft minigame, Bedwars. It builds on top of my image templating pipeline, Fractyl, to deliver sleek real-time renders in a timely manner. Discord users are able to run commands via the Statalytics Discord integration, which then fetches the relevant data from Hypixel's public API and generates the appropriate image, taking into account the user's settings and given parameters.

The decision to build with Python for the Discord integration stemmed from its rich support for image manipulation and Discord integration via Pillow and discord.py respectively. Subsequent services were also built in Python to leverage the Statalytics internal shared library and reduce project complexity.

Redis streams are used for real-time communication between services and to send important notifications to subscribed team members via Discord. With guaranteed message delivery being a requirement, and due to the lightweight nature of Redis, Redis streams were the best fit for this problem.

long.heading: UX / Web Interface
long.content:
Statalytics has a user web dashboard for users to manage their settings such as account connections, theming, and timezones. The Statalytics backend integrates with Discord OAuth to provide a seamless and secure experience for the target audience. Statalytics builds on Discord's OAuth, with its own permission and subscription systems to gate access to certain functionalities.

Statalytics also has an administrator dashboard for the team to manage different aspects of Statalytics' services. It includes growth insights, real-time logs, and user data management.

long.heading: Real World Impact
long.content: The Statalytics Discord integration has been added to ~4000 Discord servers and has served ~1 million requests since launch. Users depend on functionalities such as stat projection and periodic stat tracking.

long.heading: Lessons and Evolution
long.content:
Statalytics was my first ever and longest running actively maintained project, and with a real user base, has demanded more of my focus to deliver improvements. Because of its evolution, I have learned the pain of technical debt and have spent more time rewriting parts of services (accounts, rendering) than shipping new features. This project was the driver of my initial experiences with version control, containerization, web development, and maintainable code, laying the foundation for other projects that I have worked on.

Many aspects of this project have been iterated upon multiple times over the years. A good example of this is the rendering / design system. What originated as the monotonous manual positioning of elements and individual draw calls evolved into a slightly more visually consistent design with a specialized wrapper, and inspired me to create the Fractyl image templating pipeline. Enabled by the flexibility of SVGs, I was able to advance another step in rendering complexity, including visual properties like dynamic gradients and real-time theming.

description.short: IsleStats is a Discord integration that provides a range of functionality relating to the popular Minecraft server, MCC Island.

long.heading: Overview
long.content: IsleStats is a Discord integration that generates game stat cards for the popular Minecraft server, MCCI. It iterates upon the lessons I learnt while working on my other project, Statalytics, which has resulted in a more polished product. Inspired by earlier Statalytics rendering systems, it employs its own rendering wrapper around the Python Pillow library. IsleStats also has an easy to use web interface for managing both account and guild settings - this eliminates the friction and limitations of Discord's UI when managing complex settings. While the technical aspects of this project were primarily a solo endeavor, I worked closely with a friend who acted as a UX consultant so that the project could best serve its target audience.

long.heading: Real World Impact
long.content: The primary motivator for starting this project was the release of MCCI's public API which created a vacuum that needed to be filled. With IsleStats being one of the earliest products on the market, it was widely adopted by Discord servers, having been added to ~1000 Discord servers and invoked ~200,000 times. With advanced features such as automatic role assignment, guilds become dependent on it and as such I have worked closely with feedback from guild owners in determining the direction the project should take.

long.heading: Tooling
long.content:
The decision to use Python for this project came from my own familiarity and the ecosystem around Discord integration and image manipulation. It was vital for the success of the product that a beta release be shipped early on, and using Python for this project made that possible. The website is built in Next.js and communicates with a FastAPI service, allowing the modularity and scalability of React with the convenience of a shared internal Python library for managing data.

MongoDB was the database of choice not only because I wanted to familiarize myself with the technology, but also due to its flexibility in how data could be structured.

long.heading: Lessons
long.content: Throughout the duration of this project, I became familiar with many new technologies - Next.js, FastAPI, MongoDB, GraphQL and Tailwind. I got hands on experience with integrating different technologies in a decoupled and maintainable manner. I faced challenges with product terminology throughout the development of this project and learnt the importance of creating concrete naming conventions before shipping features. Otherwise, naming will naturally evolve, leading to inconsistencies and confusion for end users. This project highlighted the importance of good documentation and tips throughout the product - things that seem obvious to the developer may not be so obvious to the end user.

description.short: Enotify is a Discord integration that delivers alerts of new emails to a user's DMs within 10 seconds of receipt.

long.heading: Overview
long.content: Enotify is a Discord integration that bridges the gap between Gmail and Discord, delivering alerts of new emails to a user's DMs within 10 seconds of receipt. Through the web dashboard, users can add multiple Gmail accounts and filter which emails they want to receive alerts for via whitelist and blacklist settings. This project was primarily built as a personal tool and due to obvious privacy concerns, I have created a guide to self-hosting Enotify entirely on isolated infrastructure.

long.heading: Tooling
long.content: Enotify is built in Python and integrates with Google Cloud Pub/Sub to receive real time inbox updates without the need for continuous polling. There are three main components of this project. A web interface for managing connected email accounts and filters, a webhook for receiving and handling Google Cloud Pub/Sub events, and an inbox watch loop that re-validates credentials efficiently in batches. The web interface is able to indicate when credentials are invalid and an account must be re-authorized.

long.heading: Lessons
long.content:
Due to the sensitive nature of the data that Enotify must access, security was a large priority. This project provided my initial experiences with encryption, JWT validation, secure OAuth flows, and CSRF prevention. This project iterated on an initial prototype script that polled the Gmail API, and aimed to provide a more reliable and scalable experience. I was subjected to fragmented and inconsistent Google Cloud documentation and often had to fill in the gaps through trial and error.

Service to service communication is also a vital part of this project as the web server must notify the Discord integration service of new emails. This problem was solved with a bare-bones socket server system however if I were to redo this project, I would use something such as Redis streams or Redis Pub/Sub for increased flexibility and reliability.

description.short: Fractyl is a pipeline for turning figma designs into SVG templates, exporting, and rendering them with actual data.

long.heading: Overview
long.content: Fractyl is a templating pipeline for exporting Figma designs as SVG templates and dynamically rendering them with actual content on demand. It aims to solve the pain points I faced while developing my other rendering heavy projects (Statalytics, IsleStats), such as manually specifying pixel positions for text and images. Through the Figma plugin, users can mark elements as dynamic text, shapes, or images, assign an ID, and give them a value at render time. A design can be selected and exported, which splits the design into dynamic SVG fragments, rasterizes the static content, and generates a schema file that specifies the composition of the design. More advanced features include: masks for background clipping, scale variant exports, and variable exports. Because of such flexibility, the Fractyl rendering pipeline has many applications, including game stat cards, social media cards, receipts, and marketing assets.

long.heading: Renderer
long.content: Rust was the optimal choice for the renderer due to its speed and support for SVG rendering via resvg. The renderer can either be used as a standalone HTTP server for requesting renders or called directly from other Rust code as a crate. It is designed to be as simple as possible to set up while still giving flexibility to advanced users. To render a template with actual values, the render method can be called with a mapping of placeholder IDs with their respective values.

long.heading: Lessons and Motivations
long.content:
The core philosophy behind this project is that the render call should be possible without any knowledge of the visual design aspects of the template. Fonts can be scaled with "em" units, dynamic colors can be specified with exported Figma variables (`{variable:x}`), and background images will be automatically scaled and applied. This limitation gave the project a clear direction and required creative thinking to solve unique problems.

To create a pipeline with as little friction as possible, it was critical that I iterated on conceptual ideas before implementation. I decided to use SVGs as templates as it serves as a middle-ground between headless browser rendering and tedious manual positioning, with Figma doing the heavy lifting in terms of positioning and alignment. The schema was carefully crafted with foresight to allow automatic migration between different versions sequentially. It is a crucial component as it bridges the gap between the two core domains: the Figma plugin and the renderer.

description.short: Pulse is a self-contained realtime messaging platform for the web.

long.heading: Overview
long.content: Pulse is a simple real-time messaging web app. While this project has working instant messaging functionality, the core focus of this project was to develop my skills in areas such as secure authentication, horizontally scalable systems, and real-time communication. Pulse allows users to create an account and chat with other users either privately or in group chats. Pulse is largely unfinished and was never intended to be used in the real world, however it was an extremely valuable learning experience for me.

long.heading: Architecture
long.content:
There are three main layers to Pulse: a PostgreSQL database wrapped by a REST API, an API layer, and the React front-end.

The database wrapper is built in Rust and designed to provide a stateless gateway for manipulating database entries in a predefined and consistent manner across services. It provides an additional layer of security as data can't be arbitrarily read and written - only a select few operations are permitted. A range of integration tests ensure that all operations behave as expected under different circumstances. The database wrapper has minimal validation as that is the responsibility of the database schema and API business logic and because the database wrapper is stateless, it can be easily horizontally scaled without issue.

The API layer is also built in Rust with functionality such as account creation and authentication using REST endpoints and messaging providing an additional websocket based interface. To make horizontal scaling possible, I used Redis Pub/Sub for fan-out on messaging events. This allows users in a single chat to be connected to separate API nodes and still receive messages in real-time. The API securely manages authentication by salting and hashing with Argon2, and storing AES 256 GCM encrypted email addresses alongside their HMAC-SHA256 hashes. I stored hashed email addresses because AES 256 GCM encryption is non deterministic. Hashing provides a deterministic output and allows querying email addresses without the need for decryption.

Pulse also implements a session management system from scratch, supporting multiple simultaneous sessions with limited lifetimes and the ability to be revoked. Session tokens are stored on the database in SHA256 hash form such that only the client knows the true value.

long.heading: Lessons
long.content:
While the RESTful database wrapper makes it trivial to manipulate data in a predefined, structured manner, it also adds complexity and latency. In future projects, I would instead create an internal Rust crate for database operations so that the API can directly connect to the database. This serves as a good middle-ground as it still wraps the complex database query logic. Because all of the server-side code for this project is in Rust, this would work well and decrease infrastructure cost. This would also eliminate the need for the shared 'models' crate that the database wrapper and API currently depend on as a single source of truth.

While developing the database wrapper, I experienced the pain of writing comprehensive integration tests to ensure functionality behaved as expected. I was forced to build on top of Rust's existing testing framework and iterate to make tests less verbose and as easy to read as possible. This project gave me experience with more complex database schemas, unlike with past projects, with Pulse I ensured stricter types, defaults, and deletion policies to ensure data consistency and keep orphaned data to a minimum.

With websockets being a significant component of the API layer, I should have created better infrastructure around them so that defining handlers would become modular and more maintainable. This is one of the biggest issues with the API layer, and makes it difficult to decouple websocket logic from Redis fanout logic. A better approach would use a similar style to Axum's routing where handlers are defined independently and then registered in a single place in the core app.
